n: The chronicler’s story begins not with Saul’s rise but with his fall. Israel is routed by the Philistines on Mount Gilboa, about 1010 BC—setting the stage for David.

f.g: A ridge on the southeast edge of the Jezreel Valley in northern Israel.

n: Saul’s sons, including the noble Jonathan, David’s dearest friend, are killed in the battle.
The fighting turns against Saul, and enemy archers badly wound him.

f.g: Went badly for Saul; pressed hard against him.

n: Fearing torture and mockery by the Philistines, Saul asks his armor-bearer to kill him. When he refuses, Saul falls on his own sword—a tragic end for Israel’s first king.

f.g: A scornful term for the Philistines, who were outside God’s covenant.

n: The armor-bearer, loyal to the end, takes his own life as well.
Saul and his sons die together. “All his house” here means his royal dynasty effectively ended, though one son, Ish-bosheth, briefly ruled afterward.
Seeing the army’s collapse, Israelites in the valley abandon their towns, and the Philistines occupy them. Saul’s defeat leaves the nation exposed.
The next day, Philistines looting the battlefield find the bodies of Saul and his sons.

f.g: To take armor and valuables from the dead, a common practice after battle.

n: They cut off Saul’s head and send news of their victory to their idols and people, treating it as a triumph of their gods over Israel’s God.

f.g: Announce the victory in their temples, as if thanking their gods.

n: Saul’s armor is placed in a pagan temple and his head hung in Dagon’s temple—a deep humiliation. Earlier, the ark had humbled Dagon in his own temple.

f.g: A grain or fertility god worshipped by the Philistines.

n: The people of Jabesh-gilead hear what has happened. Saul had rescued their town at the start of his reign, and they had not forgotten.
Their bravest men recover the bodies and give them an honorable burial, fasting for a week. Their loyalty and gratitude are a quiet bright spot in a dark chapter.
The chronicler explains why Saul died: he was unfaithful to the Lord, disobeyed His word, and even consulted a medium. This is the key lesson of the chapter.

f.w: the word of the LORD, which he kept not
one that had a familiar spirit
f.g: A medium who claimed to call up the dead—the witch of Endor.

n: Saul did not seek the Lord, so the Lord turned the kingdom to David. The chronicler’s point is clear: blessing comes from seeking God, and the throne is God’s to give.

f.g: 1 Samuel 28:6 says Saul did ask but received no answer; the chronicler means he did not truly seek God in faith and obedience.
